eduSections.title: Why Are Business Bankruptcies Rising?
eduSections.content: Business bankruptcies in 2026 are at their highest level in over a decade. High interest rates, tightening credit markets, and lingering effects of pandemic-era debt have pushed thousands of small businesses toward insolvency. Many business owners are searching for bankruptcy options for small business - but filing isn't always the best path forward.

eduSections.title: Types of Company Bankruptcies
eduSections.content:
Chapter 7 (Liquidation): The business ceases operations. Assets are sold to pay creditors. This is the most common form of small business bankruptcies, but it means closing your doors permanently.

Chapter 11 (Reorganization): The business continues operating under a court-approved repayment plan. Expensive (legal fees often exceed $50,000) and time-consuming (12-18 months minimum).

Chapter 13 (Individual): Available only to sole proprietors. Creates a 3-5 year repayment plan. Not available for LLCs or corporations.

eduSections.title: The Alternative: Business Debt Settlement
eduSections.content: For business owners wondering how to resolve business debt without destroying their future, debt settlement offers a private, faster, and less damaging alternative. Instead of court filings and public records, we negotiate directly with your creditors to reduce what you owe - typically by 50-80%.

guideSections.title: Chapter 7 vs Chapter 11 vs Chapter 13: Which Business Bankruptcy Type Applies to You?
guideSections.content:
When considering business bankruptcy, understanding the three main types is critical. Each chapter serves a different purpose and has different eligibility requirements depending on your business structure.

Chapter 7 (Liquidation) is the most common form of small business bankruptcies. The court appoints a trustee who sells your business assets to pay creditors. Once complete, remaining eligible debts are discharged. The catch: your business ceases to exist.

Chapter 11 (Reorganization) lets you keep operating while restructuring debt under a court-approved plan. It's the most complex and expensive form of company bankruptcy, typically costing $50,000-$200,000+ in legal fees.

Chapter 13 (Individual Reorganization) is only available to sole proprietors (not LLCs or corporations). It creates a 3-5 year repayment plan based on your income.

guideSections.title: The True Cost of Filing for Business Bankruptcy
guideSections.content:
Many business owners underestimate the total cost of filing business bankruptcy. Beyond the obvious attorney fees, there are court costs, administrative expenses, and significant hidden costs.

Chapter 7 costs: Filing fee ($338) + attorney fees ($1,500-$5,000 for simple cases, $10,000+ for complex). Total: $2,000-$15,000. But the real cost is losing your entire business.

Chapter 11 costs: Filing fee ($1,738) + attorney fees ($15,000-$200,000+) + quarterly trustee fees + accountant fees. Total: $50,000-$250,000+.

Debt settlement comparison: No upfront fees. No court costs. No public record. Settle your business debt for 50-80% less than you owe, typically resolved in 3-6 months.

guideSections.title: How Business Bankruptcy Affects Your Personal Credit
guideSections.content:
If you signed a personal guarantee on any business loan, line of credit, or MCA advance (which most small business owners have), your personal credit is directly tied to that debt. A business bankruptcy involving personally guaranteed debts will appear on your personal credit report.

Bankruptcy typically drops your personal credit score by 150-250 points. Chapter 7 stays on your report for 10 years. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years.

With debt settlement: Your credit may dip temporarily during negotiations (typically 50-100 points), but begins recovering as soon as debts are settled. Most clients see recovery within 12-24 months.

guideSections.title: Business Bankruptcy Timeline: What to Expect
guideSections.content:
Chapter 7 Timeline (3-6 months): Filing, automatic stay, 341 meeting of creditors (30-45 days), trustee liquidates assets (30-90 days), discharge. But your business is gone.

Chapter 11 Timeline (12-36 months): Filing, automatic stay, disclosure statement (2-4 months), creditor negotiations (3-6 months), plan confirmation (1-3 months), ongoing execution.

Chapter 13 Timeline (3-5 years): Filing, automatic stay, plan proposal, confirmation hearing, 3-5 years of monthly payments.

Debt settlement timeline (3-6 months): Free consultation, debt analysis, creditor negotiations, settlements reached, debts resolved. No court dates, no trustees.

guideSections.title: Industries Most Affected by Business Bankruptcies in 2026
guideSections.content:
Business bankruptcies in 2026 are not hitting all industries equally. Restaurants and food service have seen filings increase 38% year-over-year due to elevated lease costs and unsustainable MCA payments.

Retail continues facing pressure from e-commerce. Construction companies that took multiple MCAs to bridge cash flow gaps are among the most common seeking bankruptcy alternatives.

Trucking and transportation have been hit by fuel cost volatility, insurance increases, and freight rate declines. Healthcare practices that expanded during 2020-2022 are carrying debt loads that don't match current revenue.

guideSections.title: What Happens to Your Employees When You File Business Bankruptcy
guideSections.content:
Chapter 7 (Liquidation): All employees are terminated. The WARN Act requires 60 days notice for 100+ employees. Unpaid wages become priority claims but employees often wait months for partial payment.

Chapter 11 (Reorganization): You can keep employees during reorganization, but uncertainty causes key staff to leave. The court may require workforce reductions.

With debt settlement: Your business keeps operating normally. Employees keep their jobs, benefits, and stability. Your team never needs to know about the debt negotiation process.

guideSections.title: Alternatives to Business Bankruptcy Beyond Debt Settlement
guideSections.content:
Debt consolidation combines multiple debts into one payment but does NOT reduce what you owe. Business restructuring means renegotiating terms directly, but creditors have little incentive to negotiate with individuals.

SBA disaster loans offer low interest rates but have limited availability and strict eligibility. Asset-based lending uses equipment or receivables as collateral but adds more debt.

Debt settlement is the only approach that actually reduces your total debt burden (by 50-80%) without court involvement, public record, or business closure.

guideSections.title: Glossary of Business Bankruptcy Terms
guideSections.content:
Automatic Stay: A court order that stops creditors from collecting once bankruptcy is filed.
Discharge: The court order eliminating your legal obligation to pay certain debts.
Liquidation: Selling business assets to pay creditors (Chapter 7).
Reorganization: Restructuring debts under court supervision (Chapter 11).
Creditor Committee: Group of largest unsecured creditors in Chapter 11 cases.
Means Test: Calculation for Chapter 7 eligibility based on income.
Preference Payment: Payments to creditors within 90 days before filing that can be clawed back.
Personal Guarantee: Your personal promise to repay business debt, exposing personal assets.
341 Meeting: Mandatory hearing where trustee and creditors question the debtor under oath.
Debt Settlement: Private negotiation to accept a reduced payment. No court, no public record.
